ADU218 wire-framing determination
=================================
Device: Ontrak ADU218, USB 0a07:00da, serial E02246
Access: stdlib fcntl.ioctl USBDEVFS_BULK on EP 0x01 (OUT) / 0x81 (IN)
State:  read-only with respect to relays; only PK was ever sent

Question: is the leading 0x01 byte a required report prefix, or incidental?

Why this needed re-measuring
----------------------------
An earlier trial appeared to show bare ASCII working. It did not: the response
read after the bare-ASCII write was the PREVIOUS prefixed command's answer,
still queued on EP 0x81. Interrupt-IN responses persist until read, so any
framing experiment that does not drain the endpoint first will credit the
wrong command. Every trial below drains EP 0x81 to empty (250 ms reads until
ETIMEDOUT) before writing, so a response can only belong to the command just
sent.

Trials (each 8 bytes, NUL-padded)
---------------------------------
  A  b'\x01PK'  -> b'\x01000\x00\x00\x00\x00'   ANSWERED
  B  b'PK'      -> TIMEOUT (errno 110)          SILENT
  C  b'PK'      -> TIMEOUT (errno 110)          SILENT   (B is repeatable)
  D  b'\x00PK'  -> TIMEOUT (errno 110)          SILENT
  E  b'\x02PK'  -> TIMEOUT (errno 110)          SILENT
  F  b'\x01PK'  -> b'\x01000\x00\x00\x00\x00'   ANSWERED (control: link healthy)

Conclusions
-----------
1. The 0x01 prefix is MANDATORY. Bare ASCII is silently ignored.
2. It is specifically 0x01, not "any non-ASCII lead byte": 0x00 and 0x02 are
   both ignored just as bare ASCII is. So the driver must send the literal
   byte, and a test asserting "first byte is not an ASCII letter" would pass
   for encodings the device rejects.
3. Responses also carry the 0x01 prefix, so the reply is not simply an echo of
   the request framing choice - both directions are prefixed.
4. Bad framing behaves exactly like an unknown command: silence, no error, and
   no lasting harm. Trial F answers normally straight after four rejections.
   Combined with errors.txt, this means SILENCE IS THE DEVICE'S ONLY ERROR
   SIGNAL - it cannot distinguish "I did not understand the bytes" from "I did
   not understand the command" from "this command has no reply".

Cross-check against the in-tree kernel driver
---------------------------------------------
Linux carries a driver for this exact device: drivers/usb/misc/adutux.c binds
vendor 0x0a07 with product 0x0064+118 = 0x00da, commented /* ADU218 */. Its
write() copies the user buffer straight to the interrupt-OUT endpoint and adds
no header, and its read() returns the interrupt payload unmodified. So a
process talking through /dev/usb/adutuxN must send the same 0x01-prefixed
8-byte packets measured above, and receives the same prefixed replies.

That is what licenses one command encoder for both access paths: the framing
is a property of the device, not of the route to it.

ADDENDUM: this file never recorded its own read timeout
------------------------------------------------------
Trials A-F above report TIMEOUT as the evidence that a prefix is
rejected, but nowhere state the timeout used, and the number is not
recoverable from the transcript. Since silence is this device's only
error signal, that value IS the measurement -- too short and a slow
answer reads as a rejection, which would have made B-E false and the
mandatory-0x01 conclusion unfounded. Recording the verdict without the
threshold that produced it left the file's central claim unfalsifiable.

Closed by re-measurement rather than by recollection, in latency.txt:

  - Observed round trip for an ANSWERED command: max 16.65 ms over 400
    samples (200x PK, 200x RPK0), median 15.99 ms, zero short reads.
    latency_after_command.txt adds the read-back immediately following
    relay actuation -- max 16.68 ms over 40 actuations -- so there is no
    slow path hiding behind a command.
  - Re-run at a 200 ms timeout, every documented silence still reads as
    silence (RI, XYZ, RPK8, RPA4, DB9, MK9999 all ETIMEDOUT), and a
    following PK answered normally with zero replies left queued.

So a rejected prefix does not answer within at least 12x the worst
observed latency of an accepted one. Whatever timeout these trials
actually used, the separation between "answers" and "stays silent" is
three orders of magnitude wider than the measurement noise, so the
A-F verdicts stand. Any future capture of this kind should state its
timeout in the transcript.
